Step 0 findings, then one scope decision.

**Already solved — don't rebuild:**
- Per-config identity is an existing pattern (`Debug`→"Workroom Dev", `Nightly`→"Workroom Nightly", `project.yml:277-305`). Per-worktree is a 4th instance of it, not a new mechanism. **[Layer 1]**
- `/usr/bin/shlock` ships with macOS — pid-file locking with stale detection, exactly the UI-test lock. Hand-rolled `mkdir` + `kill -0` was reinventing it. **[Layer 1]**
- `Scripts/channel-helper.sh` + `channel-helper_test.sh` = existing testable-shell-helper idiom. The slug logic belongs there, not inline in the Makefile.
- `UITestFixture.applyFixtureDefaults` already pins the three racing keys.
- `internal/config/config.go:82-107` already writes via `CreateTemp` + `Rename` — atomic, so two dev apps can lose an update but cannot corrupt the file.
- Build-artifact isolation: already done, zero work.

**Search check:** XcodeGen 2.46 supports `${VAR}` spec substitution, but a known issue is it not reaching `info.properties` — so use it in `settings:` only. `TEST_RUNNER_<VAR>` is the documented xcodebuild mechanism for injecting env into the test host (prefix stripped). The XCTest headers confirm the problem statement: "If the application is already running, the launch call will first terminate the existing instance."

**One correction to my own plan:** the ⌘§/⌥§ hotkey conflict does not exist. `WorkroomApp.swift:408` compiles hotkey registration out under `#if !DEBUG` — Debug builds never claim them. That bullet comes out.

**Complexity check triggers: ~31 files.** 25 of them are UI-test files, and every one of those is churn from a single decision (app-side `HOME`), not from the worktree isolation itself.

questions.question: D3 — The plan is ~31 files; 25 are UI-test churn. Reduce? ELI10: per-worktree bundle ids already give each worktree its own preferences domain, which is what was racing. Redirecting HOME on top of that buys per-run freshness. For unit tests that costs one Makefile line. For UI tests the app-under-test only takes env through XCUIApplication.launchEnvironment, so it means editing all 25 launchedApp() helpers — six-sevenths of the diff for the smallest remaining slice of isolation. Separately, those 25 near-identical helpers are real duplication worth killing on DRY grounds alone. Stakes if we pick wrong: a 31-file diff where 25 files are mechanical is hard to review, and a mistake in the shared helper breaks every UI test at once; too small and UI runs keep writing three pinned keys into that worktree's Dev domain. Recommendation: C — ship parallel-safety in a small reviewable diff, book the helper refactor as its own change where breaking every UI test is the only thing under review. Completeness: A=7/10, B=10/10, C=10/10 across two commits. Net: A is the smallest thing that makes worktrees safe; B does everything at once; C gets both with reviewable diffs. <gstack-qid:plan-eng-review-scope-reduction>

Commit 2 = shared UI-test launch helper + launchEnvironment HOME (human: ~1 day / CC: ~25 min). ✅ Parallel worktrees work after commit 1, so you unblock the actual goal immediately. ✅ The 25-file mechanical change lands alone, where a regression is unambiguous and bisectable. ❌ Two review passes instead of one, and until commit 2 a UI run still writes the 3 pinned keys into that worktree's Dev domain.

options.label: A: core only
options.description: Ship the ~7-file core; no UI-test file changes at all, ever. ✅ Smallest diff that makes concurrent worktrees safe — identity, lock, temp dir, unit-test HOME. ✅ Leaves the proven fixture-pinning seam untouched, so no risk of breaking 25 UI test classes. ❌ Leaves 25 duplicated launchedApp() helpers in place and no per-run HOME for UI tests — the pollution is per-worktree now, but still real.

options.label: B: everything in one change
options.description: Core plus the shared helper and launchEnvironment HOME in a single commit (human: ~2 days / CC: ~40 min). ✅ Full hermeticity and the DRY cleanup land together, one review, one verification pass. ✅ No window where UI tests behave differently from unit tests. ❌ A 31-file diff where a shared-helper mistake breaks all 25 classes simultaneously, and the mechanical churn buries the 6 files that carry the actual architecture.

63	
64	Every finding MUST include a confidence score (1-10):
65	
66	| Score | Meaning | Display rule |
67	|-------|---------|-------------|
68	| 9-10 | Verified by reading specific code. Concrete bug or exploit demonstrated. | Show normally |
69	| 7-8 | High confidence pattern match. Very likely correct. | Show normally |
70	| 5-6 | Moderate. Could be a false positive. | Show with caveat: "Medium confidence, verify this is actually an issue" |
71	| 3-4 | Low confidence. Pattern is suspicious but may be fine. | Suppress from main report. Include in appendix only. |
72	| 1-2 | Speculation. | Only report if severity would be P0. |

75

85	
86	1. **Quote the specific code line that motivates the finding** — file:line plus
87	   the verbatim text of the line(s) that triggered it. If the finding is "field
88	   X doesn't exist on model Y", quote the lines of class Y where the field
89	   would live. If "dict.get() might return None", quote the dict initialization.
90	   If "race condition between A and B", quote both A and B.
91	
92	2. **If you cannot quote the motivating line(s), the finding is unverified.**
93	   Force its confidence to 4-5 (suppressed from the main report). It still goes
94	   into the appendix so reviewers can audit calibration, but the user does NOT
95	   see it in the critical-pass output. Do not work around this by inventing
96	   speculative confidence 7+ — that defeats the gate.

98	**Framework-meta nudge:** When the symbol is generated by a framework
99	metaclass, descriptor, ORM Meta inner-class, or migration history (Django
100	`Meta`, Rails `has_many`/`scope`, SQLAlchemy `relationship`/`Column`,
101	TypeORM decorators, Sequelize `init`/`belongsTo`, Prisma generated client),
102	quote the meta-construct (the `Meta` block, the migration, the decorator,
103	the schema file) instead of expecting the literal name in the class body.
104	The verification is "I read the source that creates this symbol", not "I
105	grep'd for the name and didn't find it." Deeper framework-aware verification
106	(model introspection, migration-history-aware checks, ORM dialect detection)

111	
112	| FP class | Why the gate catches it |
113	|---|---|
114	| "field doesn't exist on model" | Requires quoting the model class body or Meta; the field's absence becomes obvious |
115	| "dict.get() might be None" | Requires quoting the dict initialization (e.g. Django form's `cleaned_data` is `{}`-initialized) |
116	| "save() might lose fields" | Requires quoting the ORM signature or model definition |
117	| "update_fields might miss X" | Requires quoting the field set; if X doesn't exist, the FP is self-evident |

138	
139	100% coverage is the goal. Evaluate every codepath in the plan and ensure the plan includes tests for each one. If the plan is missing tests, add them — the plan should be complete enough that implementation includes full test coverage from the start.
140	
141	### Test Framework Detection
142	
143	Before analyzing coverage, detect the project's test framework:
144	
145	1. **Read CLAUDE.md** — look for a `## Testing` section with test command and framework name. If found, use that as the authoritative source.
146	2. **If CLAUDE.md has no testing section, auto-detect:**
147	
148	```bash
149	setopt +o nomatch 2>/dev/null || true  # zsh compat
150	# Detect project runtime
151	[ -f Gemfile ] && echo "RUNTIME:ruby"
152	[ -f package.json ] && echo "RUNTIME:node"
153	[ -f requirements.txt ] || [ -f pyproject.toml ] && echo "RUNTIME:python"
154	[ -f go.mod ] && echo "RUNTIME:go"
155	[ -f Cargo.toml ] && echo "RUNTIME:rust"
156	# Check for existing test infrastructure
157	ls jest.config.* vitest.config.* playwright.config.* cypress.config.* .rspec pytest.ini phpunit.xml 2>/dev/null
158	ls -d test/ tests/ spec/ __tests__/ cypress/ e2e/ 2>/dev/null
159	```
160	
161	3. **If no framework detected:** still produce the coverage diagram, but skip test generation.
162	
163	**Step 1. Trace every codepath in the plan:**
164	
165	Read the plan document. For each new feature, service, endpoint, or component described, trace how data will flow through the code — don't just list planned functions, actually follow the planned execution:
166	
167	1. **Read the plan.** For each planned component, understand what it does and how it connects to existing code.
168	2. **Trace data flow.** Starting from each entry point (route handler, exported function, event listener, component render), follow the data through every branch:
169	   - Where does input come from? (request params, props, database, API call)
170	   - What transforms it? (validation, mapping, computation)
171	   - Where does it go? (database write, API response, rendered output, side effect)
172	   - What can go wrong at each step? (null/undefined, invalid input, network failure, empty collection)
173	3. **Diagram the execution.** For each changed file, draw an ASCII diagram showing:
174	   - Every function/method that was added or modified
175	   - Every conditional branch (if/else, switch, ternary, guard clause, early return)
176	   - Every error path (try/catch, rescue, error boundary, fallback)
177	   - Every call to another function (trace into it — does IT have untested branches?)
178	   - Every edge: what happens with null input? Empty array? Invalid type?
179	
180	This is the critical step — you're building a map of every line of code that can execute differently based on input. Every branch in this diagram needs a test.
181	
182	**Step 2. Map user flows, interactions, and error states:**
183	
184	Code coverage isn't enough — you need to cover how real users interact with the changed code. For each changed feature, think through:
185	
186	- **User flows:** What sequence of actions does a user take that touches this code? Map the full journey (e.g., "user clicks 'Pay' → form validates → API call → success/failure screen"). Each step in the journey needs a test.
187	- **Interaction edge cases:** What happens when the user does something unexpected?
188	  - Double-click/rapid resubmit
189	  - Navigate away mid-operation (back button, close tab, click another link)
190	  - Submit with stale data (page sat open for 30 minutes, session expired)
191	  - Slow connection (API takes 10 seconds — what does the user see?)
192	  - Concurrent actions (two tabs, same form)
193	- **Error states the user can see:** For every error the code handles, what does the user actually experience?
194	  - Is there a clear error message or a silent failure?
195	  - Can the user recover (retry, go back, fix input) or are they stuck?
196	  - What happens with no network? With a 500 from the API? With invalid data from the server?
197	- **Empty/zero/boundary states:** What does the UI show with zero results? With 10,000 results? With a single character input? With maximum-length input?
198	
199	Add these to your diagram alongside the code branches. A user flow with no test is just as much a gap as an untested if/else.
200	
201	**Step 3. Check each branch against existing tests:**
202	
203	Go through your diagram branch by branch — both code paths AND user flows. For each one, search for a test that exercises it:
204	- Function `processPayment()` → look for `billing.test.ts`, `billing.spec.ts`, `test/billing_test.rb`
205	- An if/else → look for tests covering BOTH the true AND false path
206	- An error handler → look for a test that triggers that specific error condition
207	- A call to `helperFn()` that has its own branches → those branches need tests too
208	- A user flow → look for an integration or E2E test that walks through the journey
209	- An interaction edge case → look for a test that simulates the unexpected action
210	
211	Quality scoring rubric:
212	- ★★★  Tests behavior with edge cases AND error paths
213	- ★★   Tests correct behavior, happy path only
214	- ★    Smoke test / existence check / trivial assertion (e.g., "it renders", "it doesn't throw")
215	
216	### E2E Test Decision Matrix
217	
218	When checking each branch, also determine whether a unit test or E2E/integration test is the right tool:
219	
220	**RECOMMEND E2E (mark as [→E2E] in the diagram):**
221	- Common user flow spanning 3+ components/services (e.g., signup → verify email → first login)
222	- Integration point where mocking hides real failures (e.g., API → queue → worker → DB)
223	- Auth/payment/data-destruction flows — too important to trust unit tests alone
224	
225	**RECOMMEND EVAL (mark as [→EVAL] in the diagram):**
226	- Critical LLM call that needs a quality eval (e.g., prompt change → test output still meets quality bar)
227	- Changes to prompt templates, system instructions, or tool definitions
228	
229	**STICK WITH UNIT TESTS:**
230	- Pure function with clear inputs/outputs
231	- Internal helper with no side effects
232	- Edge case of a single function (null input, empty array)
233	- Obscure/rare flow that isn't customer-facing

235	### REGRESSION RULE (mandatory)
236	
237	**IRON RULE:** When the coverage audit identifies a REGRESSION — code that previously worked but the diff broke — a regression test is added to the plan as a critical requirement. No AskUserQuestion. No skipping. Regressions are the highest-priority test because they prove something broke.
238	
239	A regression is when:
240	- The diff modifies existing behavior (not new code)
241	- The existing test suite (if any) doesn't cover the changed path
242	- The change introduces a new failure mode for existing callers
243	
244	When uncertain whether a change is a regression, err on the side of writing the test.

334	After all review sections are complete, run an independent second opinion from a

336	opt-in. Two models agreeing on a plan is stronger signal than one model's thorough
337	review. The user turns this off only by asking explicitly
338	(`gstack-config set codex_reviews disabled`).
339	
340	**Preflight — decide whether and how the outside voice runs:**
341	
342	```bash
343	# Codex preflight: one block (functions sourced here don't persist to later blocks).
344	_TEL=$(~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-config get telemetry 2>/dev/null || echo off)
345	_CODEX_CFG=$(~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-config get codex_reviews 2>/dev/null || echo enabled)

347	if [ "$_CODEX_CFG" = "disabled" ]; then
348	  _CODEX_MODE="disabled"
349	elif ! command -v codex >/dev/null 2>&1; then
350	  _CODEX_MODE="not_installed"; _gstack_codex_log_event "codex_cli_missing" 2>/dev/null || true
351	elif ! _gstack_codex_auth_probe >/dev/null 2>&1; then
352	  _CODEX_MODE="not_authed"; _gstack_codex_log_event "codex_auth_failed" 2>/dev/null || true
353	else

486	## CRITICAL RULE — How to ask questions
487	Follow the AskUserQuestion format from the Preamble above. Additional rules for plan reviews:
488	* **One issue = one AskUserQuestion call.** Never combine multiple issues into one question.
489	* Describe the problem concretely, with file and line references.
490	* Present 2-3 options, including "do nothing" where that's reasonable.
491	* For each option, specify in one line: effort (human: ~X / CC: ~Y), risk, and maintenance burden. If the complete option is only marginally more effort than the shortcut with CC, recommend the complete option.
492	* **Map the reasoning to my engineering preferences above.** One sentence connecting your recommendation to a specific preference (DRY, explicit > clever, minimal diff, etc.).
493	* Label with issue NUMBER + option LETTER (e.g., "3A", "3B").
494	* **Coverage vs kind:** for every per-issue AskUserQuestion you raise in this review, decide whether the options differ in coverage or in kind. If coverage (e.g., more tests vs fewer, complete error handling vs happy-path-only, full edge-case coverage vs shortcut), include `Completeness: N/10` on each option. If kind (e.g., architectural choice between two different systems, posture-over-posture, A/B/C where each is a different kind of thing), skip the score and add one line: `Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.` Do NOT fabricate scores on kind-differentiated questions — filler scores are worse than no score.
495	* **Zero findings:** if a section has zero findings, state "No issues, moving on" and proceed. Otherwise, use AskUserQuestion for each finding — a finding with an "obvious fix" is still a finding and still needs user approval before any change lands in the plan.

514	* **Depends on / blocked by:** Any prerequisites or ordering constraints.

531	### Worktree parallelization strategy
532	
533	Analyze the plan's implementation steps for parallel execution opportunities. This helps the user split work across git worktrees (via Claude Code's Agent tool with `isolation: "worktree"` or parallel workspaces).
534	
535	**Skip if:** all steps touch the same primary module, or the plan has fewer than 2 independent workstreams. In that case, write: "Sequential implementation, no parallelization opportunity."

539	1. **Dependency table** — for each implementation step/workstream:
540	
541	| Step | Modules touched | Depends on |
542	|------|----------------|------------|
543	| (step name) | (directories/modules, NOT specific files) | (other steps, or —) |
544	
545	Work at the module/directory level, not file level. Plans describe intent ("add API endpoints"), not specific files. Module-level ("controllers/, models/") is reliable; file-level is guesswork.

547	2. **Parallel lanes** — group steps into lanes:
548	   - Steps with no shared modules and no dependency go in separate lanes (parallel)
549	   - Steps sharing a module directory go in the same lane (sequential)

<!-- AUTO-GENERATED from review-sections.md.tmpl — do not edit directly -->
<!-- Regenerate: bun run gen:skill-docs -->
## Review Sections (after scope is agreed)

**Anti-skip rule:** Never condense, abbreviate, or skip any review section (1-4) regardless of plan type (strategy, spec, code, infra). Every section in this skill exists for a reason. "This is a strategy doc so implementation sections don't apply" is always wrong — implementation details are where strategy breaks down. If a section genuinely has zero findings, say "No issues found" and move on — but you must evaluate it.

**Anti-shortcut clause:** The plan file is the OUTPUT of the interactive review, not a substitute for it. Writing every finding into one plan write and calling ExitPlanMode without firing AskUserQuestion is the precise failure mode of the May 2026 transcript bug — the model explored, found issues, and dumped them into a deliverable rather than walking the user through them. If you have ANY non-trivial finding in any review section, the path from finding to ExitPlanMode goes THROUGH AskUserQuestion. Zero findings in every section is the only path to ExitPlanMode that bypasses AskUserQuestion. If you find yourself wanting to write a plan with findings before asking, stop and call AskUserQuestion now — that's the bug, recognize it.

## Prior Learnings

Search for relevant learnings from previous sessions:

```bash
_CROSS_PROJ=$(~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-config get cross_project_learnings 2>/dev/null || echo "unset")
echo "CROSS_PROJECT: $_CROSS_PROJ"
if [ "$_CROSS_PROJ" = "true" ]; then
  ~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-learnings-search --limit 10 --cross-project 2>/dev/null || true
else
  ~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-learnings-search --limit 10 2>/dev/null || true
fi
```

If `CROSS_PROJECT` is `unset` (first time): Use AskUserQuestion:

> gstack can search learnings from your other projects on this machine to find
> patterns that might apply here. This stays local (no data leaves your machine).
> Recommended for solo developers. Skip if you work on multiple client codebases
> where cross-contamination would be a concern.

Options:
- A) Enable cross-project learnings (recommended)
- B) Keep learnings project-scoped only

If A: run `~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-config set cross_project_learnings true`
If B: run `~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-config set cross_project_learnings false`

Then re-run the search with the appropriate flag.

If learnings are found, incorporate them into your analysis. When a review finding
matches a past learning, display:

**"Prior learning applied: [key] (confidence N/10, from [date])"**

This makes the compounding visible. The user should see that gstack is getting
smarter on their codebase over time.

### 1. Architecture review
Evaluate:
* Overall system design and component boundaries.
* Dependency graph and coupling concerns.
* Data flow patterns and potential bottlenecks.
* Scaling characteristics and single points of failure.
* Security architecture (auth, data access, API boundaries).
* Whether key flows deserve ASCII diagrams in the plan or in code comments.
* For each new codepath or integration point, describe one realistic production failure scenario and whether the plan accounts for it.
* **Distribution architecture:** If this introduces a new artifact (binary, package, container), how does it get built, published, and updated? Is the CI/CD pipeline part of the plan or deferred?

For each issue found in this section, call AskUserQuestion individually. One issue per call. Present options, state your recommendation, explain WHY. Do NOT batch multiple issues into one AskUserQuestion. Use the preamble's AskUserQuestion Format section. The AskUserQuestion call is a tool_use, not prose — call the tool directly.

**STOP.** Do NOT proceed to the next review section, edit the plan file with the proposed fix, or call ExitPlanMode until the user responds. An issue with an "obvious fix" is still an issue and still needs explicit user approval before it lands in the plan. Loading the AskUserQuestion schema via ToolSearch and then writing the recommendation as chat prose is the failure mode this gate exists to prevent.

## Confidence Calibration

Every finding MUST include a confidence score (1-10):

| Score | Meaning | Display rule |
|-------|---------|-------------|
| 9-10 | Verified by reading specific code. Concrete bug or exploit demonstrated. | Show normally |
| 7-8 | High confidence pattern match. Very likely correct. | Show normally |
| 5-6 | Moderate. Could be a false positive. | Show with caveat: "Medium confidence, verify this is actually an issue" |
| 3-4 | Low confidence. Pattern is suspicious but may be fine. | Suppress from main report. Include in appendix only. |
| 1-2 | Speculation. | Only report if severity would be P0. |

**Finding format:**

\`[SEVERITY] (confidence: N/10) file:line — description\`

Example:
\`[P1] (confidence: 9/10) app/models/user.rb:42 — SQL injection via string interpolation in where clause\`
\`[P2] (confidence: 5/10) app/controllers/api/v1/users_controller.rb:18 — Possible N+1 query, verify with production logs\`

### Pre-emit verification gate (#1539 — kills the "field doesn't exist" FP class)

Before any finding is promoted to the report, the gate requires:

1. **Quote the specific code line that motivates the finding** — file:line plus
   the verbatim text of the line(s) that triggered it. If the finding is "field
   X doesn't exist on model Y", quote the lines of class Y where the field
   would live. If "dict.get() might return None", quote the dict initialization.
   If "race condition between A and B", quote both A and B.

2. **If you cannot quote the motivating line(s), the finding is unverified.**
   Force its confidence to 4-5 (suppressed from the main report). It still goes
   into the appendix so reviewers can audit calibration, but the user does NOT
   see it in the critical-pass output. Do not work around this by inventing
   speculative confidence 7+ — that defeats the gate.

**Framework-meta nudge:** When the symbol is generated by a framework
metaclass, descriptor, ORM Meta inner-class, or migration history (Django
`Meta`, Rails `has_many`/`scope`, SQLAlchemy `relationship`/`Column`,
TypeORM decorators, Sequelize `init`/`belongsTo`, Prisma generated client),
quote the meta-construct (the `Meta` block, the migration, the decorator,
the schema file) instead of expecting the literal name in the class body.
The verification is "I read the source that creates this symbol", not "I
grep'd for the name and didn't find it." Deeper framework-aware verification
(model introspection, migration-history-aware checks, ORM dialect detection)
is deliberately out of scope for the lighter gate — see the deferred
`~/.gstack-dev/plans/1539-framework-aware-review.md` design doc.

The FP classes the gate kills (measured against Django Sprint 2.5 #1539):

| FP class | Why the gate catches it |
|---|---|
| "field doesn't exist on model" | Requires quoting the model class body or Meta; the field's absence becomes obvious |
| "dict.get() might be None" | Requires quoting the dict initialization (e.g. Django form's `cleaned_data` is `{}`-initialized) |
| "save() might lose fields" | Requires quoting the ORM signature or model definition |
| "update_fields might miss X" | Requires quoting the field set; if X doesn't exist, the FP is self-evident |

**Calibration learning:** If you report a finding with confidence < 7 and the user
confirms it IS a real issue, that is a calibration event. Your initial confidence was
too low. Log the corrected pattern as a learning so future reviews catch it with
higher confidence.

### 2. Code quality review
Evaluate:
* Code organization and module structure.
* DRY violations—be aggressive here.
* Error handling patterns and missing edge cases (call these out explicitly).
* Technical debt hotspots.
* Areas that are over-engineered or under-engineered relative to my preferences.
* Existing ASCII diagrams in touched files — are they still accurate after this change?

For each issue found in this section, call AskUserQuestion individually. One issue per call. Present options, state your recommendation, explain WHY. Do NOT batch multiple issues into one AskUserQuestion. Use the preamble's AskUserQuestion Format section. The AskUserQuestion call is a tool_use, not prose — call the tool directly.

**STOP.** Do NOT proceed to the next review section, edit the plan file with the proposed fix, or call ExitPlanMode until the user responds. An issue with an "obvious fix" is still an issue and still needs explicit user approval before it lands in the plan. Loading the AskUserQuestion schema via ToolSearch and then writing the recommendation as chat prose is the failure mode this gate exists to prevent.

### 3. Test review

100% coverage is the goal. Evaluate every codepath in the plan and ensure the plan includes tests for each one. If the plan is missing tests, add them — the plan should be complete enough that implementation includes full test coverage from the start.

### Test Framework Detection

Before analyzing coverage, detect the project's test framework:

1. **Read CLAUDE.md** — look for a `## Testing` section with test command and framework name. If found, use that as the authoritative source.
2. **If CLAUDE.md has no testing section, auto-detect:**

```bash
setopt +o nomatch 2>/dev/null || true  # zsh compat
# Detect project runtime
[ -f Gemfile ] && echo "RUNTIME:ruby"
[ -f package.json ] && echo "RUNTIME:node"
[ -f requirements.txt ] || [ -f pyproject.toml ] && echo "RUNTIME:python"
[ -f go.mod ] && echo "RUNTIME:go"
[ -f Cargo.toml ] && echo "RUNTIME:rust"
# Check for existing test infrastructure
ls jest.config.* vitest.config.* playwright.config.* cypress.config.* .rspec pytest.ini phpunit.xml 2>/dev/null
ls -d test/ tests/ spec/ __tests__/ cypress/ e2e/ 2>/dev/null
```

3. **If no framework detected:** still produce the coverage diagram, but skip test generation.

**Step 1. Trace every codepath in the plan:**

Read the plan document. For each new feature, service, endpoint, or component described, trace how data will flow through the code — don't just list planned functions, actually follow the planned execution:

1. **Read the plan.** For each planned component, understand what it does and how it connects to existing code.
2. **Trace data flow.** Starting from each entry point (route handler, exported function, event listener, component render), follow the data through every branch:
   - Where does input come from? (request params, props, database, API call)
   - What transforms it? (validation, mapping, computation)
   - Where does it go? (database write, API response, rendered output, side effect)
   - What can go wrong at each step? (null/undefined, invalid input, network failure, empty collection)
3. **Diagram the execution.** For each changed file, draw an ASCII diagram showing:
   - Every function/method that was added or modified
   - Every conditional branch (if/else, switch, ternary, guard clause, early return)
   - Every error path (try/catch, rescue, error boundary, fallback)
   - Every call to another function (trace into it — does IT have untested branches?)
   - Every edge: what happens with null input? Empty array? Invalid type?

This is the critical step — you're building a map of every line of code that can execute differently based on input. Every branch in this diagram needs a test.

**Step 2. Map user flows, interactions, and error states:**

Code coverage isn't enough — you need to cover how real users interact with the changed code. For each changed feature, think through:

- **User flows:** What sequence of actions does a user take that touches this code? Map the full journey (e.g., "user clicks 'Pay' → form validates → API call → success/failure screen"). Each step in the journey needs a test.
- **Interaction edge cases:** What happens when the user does something unexpected?
  - Double-click/rapid resubmit
  - Navigate away mid-operation (back button, close tab, click another link)
  - Submit with stale data (page sat open for 30 minutes, session expired)
  - Slow connection (API takes 10 seconds — what does the user see?)
  - Concurrent actions (two tabs, same form)
- **Error states the user can see:** For every error the code handles, what does the user actually experience?
  - Is there a clear error message or a silent failure?
  - Can the user recover (retry, go back, fix input) or are they stuck?
  - What happens with no network? With a 500 from the API? With invalid data from the server?
- **Empty/zero/boundary states:** What does the UI show with zero results? With 10,000 results? With a single character input? With maximum-length input?

Add these to your diagram alongside the code branches. A user flow with no test is just as much a gap as an untested if/else.

**Step 3. Check each branch against existing tests:**

Go through your diagram branch by branch — both code paths AND user flows. For each one, search for a test that exercises it:
- Function `processPayment()` → look for `billing.test.ts`, `billing.spec.ts`, `test/billing_test.rb`
- An if/else → look for tests covering BOTH the true AND false path
- An error handler → look for a test that triggers that specific error condition
- A call to `helperFn()` that has its own branches → those branches need tests too
- A user flow → look for an integration or E2E test that walks through the journey
- An interaction edge case → look for a test that simulates the unexpected action

Quality scoring rubric:
- ★★★  Tests behavior with edge cases AND error paths
- ★★   Tests correct behavior, happy path only
- ★    Smoke test / existence check / trivial assertion (e.g., "it renders", "it doesn't throw")

### E2E Test Decision Matrix

When checking each branch, also determine whether a unit test or E2E/integration test is the right tool:

**RECOMMEND E2E (mark as [→E2E] in the diagram):**
- Common user flow spanning 3+ components/services (e.g., signup → verify email → first login)
- Integration point where mocking hides real failures (e.g., API → queue → worker → DB)
- Auth/payment/data-destruction flows — too important to trust unit tests alone

**RECOMMEND EVAL (mark as [→EVAL] in the diagram):**
- Critical LLM call that needs a quality eval (e.g., prompt change → test output still meets quality bar)
- Changes to prompt templates, system instructions, or tool definitions

**STICK WITH UNIT TESTS:**
- Pure function with clear inputs/outputs
- Internal helper with no side effects
- Edge case of a single function (null input, empty array)
- Obscure/rare flow that isn't customer-facing

### REGRESSION RULE (mandatory)

**IRON RULE:** When the coverage audit identifies a REGRESSION — code that previously worked but the diff broke — a regression test is added to the plan as a critical requirement. No AskUserQuestion. No skipping. Regressions are the highest-priority test because they prove something broke.

A regression is when:
- The diff modifies existing behavior (not new code)
- The existing test suite (if any) doesn't cover the changed path
- The change introduces a new failure mode for existing callers

When uncertain whether a change is a regression, err on the side of writing the test.

**Step 4. Output ASCII coverage diagram:**

Include BOTH code paths and user flows in the same diagram. Mark E2E-worthy and eval-worthy paths:

```
CODE PATHS                                            USER FLOWS
[+] src/services/billing.ts                           [+] Payment checkout
  ├── processPayment()                                  ├── [★★★ TESTED] Complete purchase — checkout.e2e.ts:15
  │   ├── [★★★ TESTED] happy + declined + timeout      ├── [GAP] [→E2E] Double-click submit
  │   ├── [GAP]         Network timeout                 └── [GAP]        Navigate away mid-payment
  │   └── [GAP]         Invalid currency
  └── refundPayment()                                 [+] Error states
      ├── [★★  TESTED] Full refund — :89                ├── [★★  TESTED] Card declined message
      └── [★   TESTED] Partial (non-throw only) — :101  └── [GAP]        Network timeout UX

LLM integration: [GAP] [→EVAL] Prompt template change — needs eval test

COVERAGE: 5/13 paths tested (38%)  |  Code paths: 3/5 (60%)  |  User flows: 2/8 (25%)
QUALITY: ★★★:2 ★★:2 ★:1  |  GAPS: 8 (2 E2E, 1 eval)
```

Legend: ★★★ behavior + edge + error  |  ★★ happy path  |  ★ smoke check
[→E2E] = needs integration test  |  [→EVAL] = needs LLM eval

**Fast path:** All paths covered → "Test review: All new code paths have test coverage ✓" Continue.

**Step 5. Add missing tests to the plan:**

For each GAP identified in the diagram, add a test requirement to the plan. Be specific:
- What test file to create (match existing naming conventions)
- What the test should assert (specific inputs → expected outputs/behavior)
- Whether it's a unit test, E2E test, or eval (use the decision matrix)
- For regressions: flag as **CRITICAL** and explain what broke

The plan should be complete enough that when implementation begins, every test is written alongside the feature code — not deferred to a follow-up.

### Test Plan Artifact

After producing the coverage diagram, write a test plan artifact to the project directory so `/qa` and `/qa-only` can consume it as primary test input:

```bash
eval "$(~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-slug 2>/dev/null)" && mkdir -p ~/.gstack/projects/$SLUG
USER=$(whoami)
DATETIME=$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)
```

Write to `~/.gstack/projects/{slug}/{user}-{branch}-eng-review-test-plan-{datetime}.md`:

```markdown
# Test Plan
Generated by /plan-eng-review on {date}
Branch: {branch}
Repo: {owner/repo}

## Affected Pages/Routes
- {URL path} — {what to test and why}

## Key Interactions to Verify
- {interaction description} on {page}

## Edge Cases
- {edge case} on {page}

## Critical Paths
- {end-to-end flow that must work}
```

This file is consumed by `/qa` and `/qa-only` as primary test input. Include only the information that helps a QA tester know **what to test and where** — not implementation details.

For LLM/prompt changes: check the "Prompt/LLM changes" file patterns listed in CLAUDE.md. If this plan touches ANY of those patterns, state which eval suites must be run, which cases should be added, and what baselines to compare against. Then use AskUserQuestion to confirm the eval scope with the user.

For each issue found in this section, call AskUserQuestion individually. One issue per call. Present options, state your recommendation, explain WHY. Do NOT batch multiple issues into one AskUserQuestion. Use the preamble's AskUserQuestion Format section. The AskUserQuestion call is a tool_use, not prose — call the tool directly.

**STOP.** Do NOT proceed to the next review section, edit the plan file with the proposed fix, or call ExitPlanMode until the user responds. ## CRITICAL RULE — How to ask questions
Follow the AskUserQuestion format from the Preamble above. Additional rules for plan reviews:
* **One issue = one AskUserQuestion call.** Never combine multiple issues into one question.
* Describe the problem concretely, with file and line references.
* Present 2-3 options, including "do nothing" where that's reasonable.
* For each option, specify in one line: effort (human: ~X / CC: ~Y), risk, and maintenance burden. If the complete option is only marginally more effort than the shortcut with CC, recommend the complete option.
* **Map the reasoning to my engineering preferences above.** One sentence connecting your recommendation to a specific preference (DRY, explicit > clever, minimal diff, etc.).
* Label with issue NUMBER + option LETTER (e.g., "3A", "3B").
* **Coverage vs kind:** for every per-issue AskUserQuestion you raise in this review, decide whether the options differ in coverage or in kind. If coverage (e.g., more tests vs fewer, complete error handling vs happy-path-only, full edge-case coverage vs shortcut), include `Completeness: N/10` on each option. If kind (e.g., architectural choice between two different systems, posture-over-posture, A/B/C where each is a different kind of thing), skip the score and add one line: `Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.` Do NOT fabricate scores on kind-differentiated questions — filler scores are worse than no score.
* **Zero findings:** if a section has zero findings, state "No issues, moving on" and proceed. Otherwise, use AskUserQuestion for each finding — a finding with an "obvious fix" is still a finding and still needs user approval before any change lands in the plan.

## Required outputs

### "NOT in scope" section
Every plan review MUST produce a "NOT in scope" section listing work that was considered and explicitly deferred, with a one-line rationale for each item.

### "What already exists" section
List existing code/flows that already partially solve sub-problems in this plan, and whether the plan reuses them or unnecessarily rebuilds them.

### TODOS.md updates
After all review sections are complete, present each potential TODO as its own individual AskUserQuestion. Never batch TODOs — one per question. Never silently skip this step. Follow the format in `.claude/skills/review/TODOS-format.md`.

For each TODO, describe:
* **What:** One-line description of the work.
* **Why:** The concrete problem it solves or value it unlocks.
* **Pros:** What you gain by doing this work.
* **Cons:** Cost, complexity, or risks of doing it.
* **Context:** Enough detail that someone picking this up in 3 months understands the motivation, the current state, and where to start.
* **Depends on / blocked by:** Any prerequisites or ordering constraints.

Then present options: **A)** Add to TODOS.md **B)** Skip — not valuable enough **C)** Build it now in this PR instead of deferring.

Do NOT just append vague bullet points. A TODO without context is worse than no TODO — it creates false confidence that the idea was captured while actually losing the reasoning.

### Diagrams
The plan itself should use ASCII diagrams for any non-trivial data flow, state machine, or processing pipeline. Additionally, identify which files in the implementation should get inline ASCII diagram comments — particularly Models with complex state transitions, Services with multi-step pipelines, and Concerns with non-obvious mixin behavior.

### Failure modes
For each new codepath identified in the test review diagram, list one realistic way it could fail in production (timeout, nil reference, race condition, stale data, etc.) and whether:
1. A test covers that failure
2. Error handling exists for it
3. The user would see a clear error or a silent failure

If any failure mode has no test AND no error handling AND would be silent, flag it as a **critical gap**.

### Worktree parallelization strategy

Analyze the plan's implementation steps for parallel execution opportunities. This helps the user split work across git worktrees (via Claude Code's Agent tool with `isolation: "worktree"` or parallel workspaces).

**Skip if:** all steps touch the same primary module, or the plan has fewer than 2 independent workstreams. In that case, write: "Sequential implementation, no parallelization opportunity."

**Otherwise, produce:**

1. **Dependency table** — for each implementation step/workstream:

| Step | Modules touched | Depends on |
|------|----------------|------------|
| (step name) | (directories/modules, NOT specific files) | (other steps, or —) |

Work at the module/directory level, not file level. Plans describe intent ("add API endpoints"), not specific files. Module-level ("controllers/, models/") is reliable; file-level is guesswork.

2. **Parallel lanes** — group steps into lanes:
   - Steps with no shared modules and no dependency go in separate lanes (parallel)
   - Steps sharing a module directory go in the same lane (sequential)
   - Steps depending on other steps go in later lanes

Format: `Lane A: step1 → step2 (sequential, shared models/)` / `Lane B: step3 (independent)`

3. **Execution order** — which lanes launch in parallel, which wait. Example: "Launch A + B in parallel worktrees. Merge both. Then C."

4. **Conflict flags** — if two parallel lanes touch the same module directory, flag it: "Lanes X and Y both touch module/ — potential merge conflict. Consider sequential execution or careful coordination."

```bash
#   SOURCE_FINDING, EFFORT_HUMAN, EFFORT_CC, FILES_JSON (a JSON array literal
#   like '["browse/src/sanitize.ts","browse/src/server.ts"]').
jq -nc \
  --arg phase 'eng-review' \
  --arg run_id "$RUN_ID" \
  --arg branch "$BRANCH" \
  --arg commit "$COMMIT" \
  --arg id "$TASK_ID" \
  --arg priority "$PRIORITY" \
  --arg component "$COMPONENT" \
  --arg effort_human "$EFFORT_HUMAN" \
  --arg effort_cc "$EFFORT_CC" \
  --arg title "$TITLE" \
  --arg source_finding "$SOURCE_FINDING" \
  --argjson files "$FILES_JSON" \

```

LEARNINGS: 10 loaded (9 pitfalls, 1 operational)

## Pitfalls
- [multigroup-prune-survivor-must-honour-former-selection] (confidence: 9/10, cross-model, 2026-07-30)
  When a per-window model goes from ONE collection to a LIST (macapp workroomSplit -> workroomSplits), every self-heal that re-points selection must know WHICH member of the list the user was viewing. AppStore.apply nils a dead selection BEFORE calling pruneWorkroomSplitToLiveLeaves, so the prune has to be handed the pre-validation selection (formerSelection:) or it picks survivors.first and lands the user in a split group they were never looking at. Claude adversarial subagent and Codex independently flagged this as the one real regression of the multi-group refactor. (files: macapp/WorkroomApp/Core/AppStore+WorkroomSplit.swift, macapp/WorkroomApp/Core/AppStore.swift)
- [focusedvalue-menu-enablement-refreshes-async-in-uitests] (confidence: 9/10, observed, 2026-07-27)
  macapp menu-item enablement flows through focusedSceneValue/@FocusedValue, which re-publishes ASYNCHRONOUSLY. An XCUITest that dismisses a dialog and immediately typeKey()s a menu shortcut races that refresh: the key equivalent lands while the item is still disabled and is silently DROPPED, with no retry, so the test fails on correct code. Fix: observe the item become enabled first (open the File menu and poll isEnabled) before sending the shortcut. Also note enablement is only queryable with the menu OPEN. (files: macapp/WorkroomAppUITests/NewWorkroomDialogUITests.swift, macapp/WorkroomApp/Views/RootView.swift)
- [pane-isSelected-is-model-focus-not-first-responder] (confidence: 9/10, observed, 2026-07-27)
  macapp PaneTreeView pane .isSelected trait tracks MODEL focus (PaneTreeView`s own `focused` = surfaceActive && tabID == focusedID), NOT the AppKit first responder. So it CANNOT be used to assert that a terminal gave up/regained keyboard focus: TerminalContainerView.isFocusedPane drives the responder while the ring/find-bar/a11y trait keep reading the model value, and a fix that resigns the responder deliberately leaves the ring up. Corrects the implication in single-pane-fixture-has-no-queryable-focus-signal — fixture-gating the trait makes single-pane MODEL focus queryable, nothing more. To assert real keyboard focus in XCUITest, type without clicking and check where the characters land (e.g. a filter field value), which is also the user-visible behaviour. (files: macapp/WorkroomApp/Views/PaneTreeView.swift, macapp/WorkroomApp/Views/TerminalContainerView.swift, macapp/WorkroomAppUITests/NewWorkroomDialogUITests.swift)
- [single-pane-fixture-has-no-queryable-focus-signal] (confidence: 9/10, observed, 2026-07-27)
  macapp PaneTreeView.swift:460 adds .isSelected only when focused && multiPane, so in the single-pane UITestFixture there is NO a11y signal for terminal keyboard focus — any XCUITest asserting the terminal has focus is vacuous. Combined with the recorded fact that synthetic events lie about focus/hover, single-pane focus behaviour is currently unverifiable at any tier. Fix by fixture-gating the trait: focused && (multiPane || UITestFixture.isActive) — fixture-gated, not unconditional, since a lone pane reporting selected to VoiceOver is wrong. (files: macapp/WorkroomApp/Views/PaneTreeView.swift)
- [isEditingTextField-makes-cmdR-behind-sheet-tests-tautological] (confidence: 9/10, cross-model, 2026-07-27)
  macapp AppStore.isEditingTextField (AppStore.swift:1557-1562, NSApp.keyWindow?.firstResponder is NSText) ALREADY guards runOrFocusRunCommand/stopSelectedRunCommand/restartSelectedRunCommand at :1595/:1638/:1646 — added by review #8 for exactly this reason. So any test asserting that Cmd-R does not fire behind a sheet with a text field (Add Project, Project Settings, Delete Project, Workroom Label) PASSES on unmodified code and proves nothing. Use Cmd-T (New Terminal), which has no such guard. It also means a focus fix that moves first responder into a dialog text field buys Cmd-R/Shift-Cmd-R/Opt-Cmd-R blocking for free. (files: macapp/WorkroomApp/Core/AppStore.swift)
- [panetreeview-contentpanel-param-shadows-content] (confidence: 9/10, cross-model, 2026-07-27)
  In macapp PaneTreeView, PaneLeafView has a stored `let content: TabContent` (:349) AND a helper `contentPanel(_ content: some View)` (:531) whose parameter shadows it. Code inside contentPanel that says `content` resolves to the View, not the TabContent, so `content.filePath` targets the wrong type and does not compile. When threading a tab-content-derived value into the footer, pass it as an explicit parameter from paneContent (where the descriptor is already in scope) rather than reading the property inside contentPanel. (files: macapp/WorkroomApp/Views/PaneTreeView.swift)
- [nshostingview-no-a11y-children-in-unit-tests] (confidence: 9/10, cross-model, 2026-07-27)
  macapp unit tests CANNOT assert SwiftUI text/labels. macOS only materializes SwiftUI a11y elements for a live AX client, so an NSHostingView in a unit-test process reports an AXGroup with 0 children (documented at HistoryCommitCardTests.swift:9-13). PaneRenderingTests works only because GhosttySurfaceView is a real NSView it can count in the AppKit hierarchy; a SwiftUI Text is not a subview and is unreachable. Do NOT plan in-gate render assertions for SwiftUI content: test the DECISION (a pure accessor/predicate) in the unit gate and leave rendering to XCUITest. Caught by Codex after a Claude review recommended the infeasible test. (files: macapp/WorkroomAppTests/HistoryCommitCardTests.swift, macapp/WorkroomAppTests/PaneRenderingTests.swift)
- [markdown-preview-reparenting-vs-deletion] (confidence: 9/10, cross-model, 2026-07-24)
  In the macapp Markdown preview (marked + DOMPurify + innerHTML), raw HTML in a .md file destroys the render two DIFFERENT ways, and a textContent-based test only sees the first: (1) raw-text/RCDATA tags (title, textarea, script, style, xmp, plaintext) make the parser absorb the rest of the doc as text, which DOMPurify then DELETES via FORBID_CONTENTS; (2) select, dialog, object, applet keep every word in the DOM but REPARENT the remainder as their children and never render them. Both look like the file is cut off. Assert that blocks after the mention are still top-level children (:scope > h2), never just textContent. Boundary: unclosed div/a/ul/li/code/details also reparent but still RENDER, and GitHub matches that, so they must stay passthrough. (files: macapp/Resources/markdown/render.js, macapp/WorkroomAppTests/MarkdownRenderPipelineTests.swift)
- [crosswindow-reload-must-clear-pending-sheets-too] (confidence: 9/10, cross-model, 2026-07-24)
  In macapp AppStore, a project/workroom-scoped pending-sheet state (pendingProjectSettings, pendingWorkroomLabel) must be invalidated in BOTH removal paths: the local synchronous delete (removeProjectLocally) AND the async reload path (apply(_:)) that every OTHER window goes through on its periodic/on-focus refresh. Fixing only removeProjectLocally leaves the identical stale-config-leak reachable via a second window whose reload drops the project but never clears its own open sheet. (files: macapp/WorkroomApp/Core/AppStore.swift)

## Operationals
- [uitestfixture-seeds-only-two-root-level-files] (confidence: 9/10, observed, 2026-07-27)
  macapp UITestFixture seeds exactly TWO real files on disk in the fake workroom: Gemfile (seededFileName, carries UITEST_FILE_MARKER) and NOTES.md (seededMarkdownFileName), both ROOT-LEVEL (UITestFixture.swift:385-392). Every other changedFiles entry (app/models/user.rb, config/routes.rb) has a CANNED DIFF but no on-disk file, so a DIFF pane renders fine while a FILE pane (PlainFileViewer reads real disk) shows an error placeholder. A UI test needing a nested path must go through the diff path, not the file path, unless it also seeds the file (the fixture already calls createDirectory withIntermediateDirectories at :379). (files: macapp/WorkroomApp/Core/UITestFixture.swift, macapp/WorkroomAppUITests/ChangesPanelUITests.swift)

content.text:
**Section 1 — Architecture review.** Four findings.

`[P1] (confidence: 9/10) macapp/project.yml:284` — `PRODUCT_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER: com.developwithstyle.workroom.dev`, a per-config constant. Verified premise: every worktree's Debug build is one app to macOS.

`[P1] (confidence: 8/10) Makefile (new slug logic)` — detection is the single point of failure, and it fails **silently**. If the "is this a secondary checkout?" test says no when it should say yes, you get the shared identity back and the races return with no signal. The jj half is unverified: this repo has no `.jj` (`test -d .jj` → absent), so `.jj/repo`-is-a-file is my claim, not a checked fact.

`[P2] (confidence: 8/10) GhosttyApp.swift:219` — `.appendingPathComponent("Workroom", isDirectory: true)` is identity-blind: release, Dev and Nightly all write one `~/Library/Application Support/Workroom/ghostty.conf`. Two dev instances with different appearances overwrite each other's theme file.

`[P2] (confidence: 7/10) project.yml:286-288 + SystemNotifier.swift:51` — `CODE_SIGN_STYLE: Automatic` / `CODE_SIGN_IDENTITY: "Apple Development"` plus `center.requestAuthorization(...)`: a brand-new bundle id per worktree is a new signing subject and a new privacy subject.

Correction to the plan: `WorkroomApp.swift:408` wraps hotkey registration in `#if !DEBUG` — Debug never claims ⌘§/⌥§, so that bullet is wrong and comes out.

questions.question: Issue 1 — Worktree detection fails silently. How should identity resolve? ELI10: the Makefile has to answer "am I a secondary checkout?" to decide whether to suffix the bundle id. Git is easy and reliable (compare git-dir against git-common-dir). For jj I am asserting that a secondary workspace has .jj/repo as a file rather than a directory, and this repo has no .jj to check against. If that guess is wrong, the build quietly uses the shared identity, both worktrees land in one preferences domain again, and the failure looks exactly like the flaky tests you started with. Stakes if we pick wrong: silent regression to the current broken state, debugged from scratch weeks later. Recommendation: 1A — an escape hatch plus a printed identity line means detection can be wrong without being invisible, and it matches your explicit-over-clever preference. Completeness: A=10/10, B=6/10, C=8/10. Net: A costs three extra lines of Makefile for a failure mode that otherwise announces itself as mystery flakes. <gstack-qid:plan-eng-review-worktree-detection>

options.label: 1A: detect + override + echo (recommended)
options.description: Auto-detect (git-dir vs git-common-dir; .jj/repo file test), honour an explicit WR_DEV_SLUG override, and echo the resolved bundle id + product name on every app-build/app-run/app-test. ✅ A wrong or missing detection is visible in the first line of build output instead of silently sharing a domain. ✅ WR_DEV_SLUG lets any layout work — jj workspaces, a plain second clone, a Docker-less CI matrix — without touching detection logic. ❌ Three more lines of Makefile shell and one more thing to keep in the docs.

options.label: 1B: auto-detect only

questions.question: Issue 2 — ghostty.conf is shared by every app identity. Scope the fix how? ELI10: GhosttyApp.swift:219 writes one file at ~/Library/Application Support/Workroom/ghostty.conf holding the resolved theme for the current appearance. The path has no identity in it, so the release app, Workroom Dev, Workroom Nightly and every worktree's dev build all write the same file. Today that mostly hides because the theme resolves to the same value; the moment two instances disagree (different appearance, different bundled theme set, mid-refactor theme code) they overwrite each other and new terminal surfaces inherit whichever wrote last. Stakes if we pick wrong: a terminal in worktree A silently picks up worktree B's colours, which reads as a theming bug in whatever you happen to be working on. Recommendation: 2A — the file is regenerated on demand and cheap, so making the path carry the bundle id fixes all identities at once instead of leaving release and nightly sharing. Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10, C=3/10. Net: A is one line for full isolation; B fixes only the case you hit today; C leaves a real cross-talk path open. <gstack-qid:plan-eng-review-ghostty-conf-path>

options.label: 2A: namespace by bundle id, all builds (recommended)
options.description: Write to Application Support/<bundle id>/ghostty.conf for every identity, release included. ✅ Every identity gets its own file — release, nightly, dev, and each worktree — with no conditional logic anywhere. ✅ The file is generated on launch and on appearance change, so the migration is "it regenerates", not "we migrate". ❌ Leaves one orphaned ~/Library/Application Support/Workroom/ghostty.conf behind on existing installs (harmless, but litter).

options.label: 2B: namespace only suffixed dev builds
options.description: Keep the shared path for release/nightly/plain-Dev; suffix only when a worktree slug is present. ✅ Zero behaviour change for the shipped app — the release path is untouched by dev tooling. ✅ Fixes the case that actually motivated this change (two worktree dev apps). ❌ Adds a conditional to a path helper and leaves release/nightly/Dev still sharing one file, so the same bug survives in a different combination.

options.label: 2C: leave it shared
options.description: Do nothing; accept theme-file cross-talk between instances. ✅ No diff, no orphaned file, no risk of breaking theme resolution. ✅ In practice both instances usually resolve the same theme, so the collision is often invisible. ❌ A real cross-instance write race stays open and will surface as an unreproducible theming bug in whichever worktree loses the race.

questions.question: Issue 3 — A new bundle id per worktree is a new signing and privacy subject. How to handle? ELI10: project.yml:286-288 signs Debug with automatic "Apple Development" signing, which means Xcode wants a registered App ID for whatever bundle id it sees. Every new worktree invents one (…workroom.dev.feat-x), so the first build there may involve Xcode talking to your developer account. Separately, macOS tracks notification permission per bundle id (SystemNotifier.swift:51 requestAuthorization), so each worktree's app is a stranger to the system and asks once. Neither is fatal, but both are first-run surprises that look like build breakage if unexpected. Stakes if we pick wrong: your first build in a fresh worktree fails on signing with a confusing message, or a permission alert pops during a UI-test run and steals focus. Recommendation: 3A — keep the normal dev signing path and fall back only if it actually errors; macOS apps with no entitlements and no sandbox generally need no provisioning profile, so this most likely never fires. Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score. Net: A verifies the cheap assumption first and documents the escape hatch; B pays a small debuggability cost up front to remove the question entirely. <gstack-qid:plan-eng-review-signing-identity>

options.label: 3A: keep Apple Development, document fallback (recommended)
options.description: Leave Debug signing as-is. Verify on the first suffixed build; if it errors, pass CODE_SIGN_IDENTITY=- CODE_SIGNING_REQUIRED=NO (the flags CI already uses per Makefile:48-51) and note it in the docs. ✅ Keeps dev builds signed the same way as today, so debugging, notarization parity and Keychain behaviour are unchanged. ✅ Costs nothing if the assumption holds, and the fallback is a documented one-liner if it does not. ❌ You find out at first build in a worktree rather than now, and the notification prompt still appears once per worktree.

options.label: 3B: ad-hoc sign suffixed builds
options.description: When a worktree slug is present, always build with CODE_SIGN_IDENTITY=- CODE_SIGNING_REQUIRED=NO. ✅ No developer-account interaction ever, so a fresh worktree builds offline and identically on any machine. ✅ Removes a whole class of "works in my main checkout" signing differences between worktrees. ❌ Ad-hoc builds differ from your primary checkout in signing, which can change Keychain access and any signature-sensitive behaviour you later debug.
